SpeedSlightly faster (no TLS handshake)Slightly slower on first connection; HTTP/2, HTTP/3 and session resumption largely remove the difference
URL prefixhttp://https:// (padlock icon in the browser)
Data safetyPasswords, card numbers and cookies can be read or modified in transit (MITM attack)Protected against eavesdropping, tampering and server impersonation
SEO / browser behaviourMarked "Not secure" by modern browsers on formsPreferred by search engines; required for geolocation, camera, service workers
Typical usePublic, non-sensitive information pagesLogin, banking, e-commerce, e-mail, APIs, all modern sites

Conclusion: HTTPS = HTTP + TLS. Since almost every site needs authentication and private data, HTTPS is now the default choice; HTTP is retained only for non-sensitive or internal documentation.

Conclusion: TCP and UDP differ in reliability versus speed — TCP is connection-oriented, ordered and acknowledged, UDP is connectionless and best-effort — and applications choose between them accordingly. HTTP and HTTPS differ in security — HTTPS is simply HTTP carried inside an SSL/TLS tunnel with certificates, so it provides confidentiality, integrity and authentication on port 443. In both pairs the “better” protocol depends on the requirement: accuracy for the transport choice and security for the Web choice.

Long 45
Question

Difference between TCP vs. UDP.

LongUnit 33.4. Difference between HTTP and HTTPS ★
opens in a full-screen window — click the question or press Enter

This answer explains the difference between TCP and UDP in detail — the features of each protocol, their headers and connection behaviour, a complete point-by-point comparison table, the applications suited to each and a decision guideline.

Definition: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) is a connection-oriented, reliable, byte-stream transport-layer protocol (RFC 793) that provides process-to-process delivery between applications using 16-bit port numbers. It is the protocol over which HTTP, FTP, SMTP, POP3, IMAP, Telnet and most Internet traffic runs.

Features
  • Connection oriented: a virtual connection is established before data transfer by the three-way handshake — SYN (seq=x) → SYN+ACK (seq=y, ack=x+1) → ACK (ack=y+1).
  • Reliable, ordered delivery: every byte is numbered; the receiver acknowledges the next expected byte; lost segments are retransmitted after a timeout or on duplicate ACKs, so data is delivered in order and without loss or duplication.
  • Flow control: sliding-window with window advertisement prevents the sender from overrunning a slow receiver.
  • Congestion control: slow start, congestion avoidance, fast retransmit/recovery; the window adapts to network load.
  • Full duplex and supports multiplexing many connections through ports; connection is closed with FIN/ACK (four-way, or RST for abort).
  • Header: 20 bytes minimum, up to 60 with options; fields — source/destination port, sequence number, acknowledgement number, data offset, flags (URG, ACK, PSH, RST, SYN, FIN), window, checksum, urgent pointer, options.

Applications: HTTP/HTTPS, FTP, SMTP/POP3/IMAP, SSH, Telnet — anything that must not lose data: file transfer, e-mail, Web pages, database access, remote login. Examples of port numbers: FTP 20/21, SSH 22, Telnet 23, SMTP 25, DNS (zone transfer) 53, HTTP 80, POP3 110, IMAP 143, HTTPS 443.

Limitations: more overhead (header + handshake + ACKs), higher latency than UDP, head-of-line blocking (a lost segment delays all later data), and no built-in encryption — security must come from TLS/IPsec.

Definition: UDP (User Datagram Protocol) is a connectionless, unreliable, best-effort transport-layer protocol (RFC 768). It simply takes the application's message, adds an 8-byte header and sends it — without any handshake, acknowledgement, retransmission or ordering.

Features
  • Connectionless: no connection setup or teardown; each datagram is independent.
  • Unreliable: datagrams may be lost, duplicated or arrive out of order; only a checksum detects corruption of the header/data.
  • Uses the port number in its header to deliver the user datagram to the correct application program at the destination (source port, destination port, length, checksum — 8 bytes total).
  • Message oriented: datagram boundaries are preserved (no byte stream, no merging).
  • Fast and lightweight: no handshake, no state, no ACKs, low header overhead; supports broadcast and multicast, which TCP cannot do.
  • No flow or congestion control: the application must handle both (or lose packets).

Applications: DNS (queries, port 53), DHCP (67/68), TFTP (69), SNMP (161), VoIP/SIP, live audio-video streaming, online gaming, broadcast/multicast, NTP (123), routing updates (RIP). Where a small loss is acceptable but delay is not, UDP is preferred; where every bit matters, TCP is used.

Difference between TCP and UDP
PointTCPUDP
Full formTransmission Control ProtocolUser Datagram Protocol
ConnectionConnection-oriented (three-way handshake)Connectionless (no handshake)
ReliabilityReliable — acknowledgements, retransmission, orderingUnreliable — best effort, no ACK
OrderingData reassembled in sequence using sequence numbersNo ordering; datagrams may arrive out of order
Speed / latencySlower (overhead of handshake, ACKs)Faster, low latency
Header size20–60 bytes8 bytes
Flow & congestion controlSliding window, slow start, congestion avoidanceNone
Broadcast / multicastNot supported (unicast only)Supported
Typical applicationsHTTP/HTTPS, FTP, SMTP, POP3, IMAP, SSH, TelnetDNS, DHCP, TFTP, SNMP, VoIP, streaming, online games
SuitabilityWhere accuracy matters more than speedWhere speed matters more than occasional loss
Remember: TCP = "talk, verify, confirm"; UDP = "shoot and forget".
Which protocol should be used? (decision guideline)
RequirementChooseReason
Every byte must arrive, order matters (file, mail, Web)TCPAcknowledgements, retransmission, sequencing
Short request/response, small messages (DNS query)UDPNo handshake overhead; retry at application level if needed
Real-time voice/video, live gamesUDPLate data is useless; delay must stay small
Broadcast/multicast deliveryUDPTCP supports only unicast
Simple device with tiny memory (sensor, TFTP client)UDPMinimal state, 8-byte header

Conclusion: TCP provides a reliable, ordered, connection-oriented byte stream with acknowledgement, retransmission, flow control and congestion control, which makes it right for Web, mail, file transfer and remote login; UDP provides a fast, connectionless, best-effort datagram service with an 8-byte header, which suits DNS, DHCP, VoIP, streaming, gaming and multicast. The two protocols complement each other, and a complete transport-layer answer should mention that TCP is used when correctness matters while UDP is used when time matters.

Long 46
Question

Difference between HTTP and HTTPS.

LongUnit 33.4. Difference between HTTP and HTTPS ★★★
opens in a full-screen window — click the question or press Enter

This answer explains the difference between HTTP and HTTPS in detail — HTTP's request–response mechanism, methods, status codes and message format, the security services added by SSL/TLS, the TLS handshake, certificates, ports, speed and practical implications.

Definition: HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) is the application-layer request–response protocol (RFC 7230-7235, and RFC 9110 for HTTP semantics) used by the World Wide Web to transfer hypertext (HTML), images, scripts, video and other resources between a client (browser/user agent) and a Web server. Default port 80 (TCP).

Features
  • Client–server, request–response: the client always initiates; the server answers with a status code + headers + body.
  • Stateless: the server keeps no memory of earlier requests — state is added with cookies, sessions and tokens.
  • Media independent and human-readable text protocol (headers are plain ASCII text).
  • Connection handling: HTTP/1.0 non-persistent (one request per TCP connection), HTTP/1.1 persistent with pipelining, HTTP/2 multiplexed over one connection in binary framing, HTTP/3 over QUIC (UDP).
  • Methods: GET, POST, HEAD, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS, PATCH, TRACE, CONNECT.
  • Status codes: 1xx information, 2xx success (200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content), 3xx redirection (301 Moved Permanently, 302 Found, 304 Not Modified), 4xx client error (400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found, 429 Too Many Requests), 5xx server error (500 Internal Server Error, 503 Service Unavailable).
Message format
  • Request: the first line is the request line = method + URL + HTTP version (for example GET /index.html HTTP/1.1), followed by header lines (Host, User-Agent, Accept, Cookie, Content-Type, Content-Length...), a blank line, and an optional body.
  • Response: a status line (HTTP/1.1 200 OK), headers (Date, Server, Content-Type, Content-Length, Set-Cookie, Cache-Control...), blank line, and the body (HTML page, image, JSON).

Limitations: plain text (no encryption → sniffing and tampering), no built-in authentication of the server, statelessness needs extra mechanisms, and it is request-response only (no server push without WebSocket/HTTP2 push). These limitations are solved by HTTPS.

Definition: SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) is a security protocol that runs between the application layer and the transport layer (it is often shown as a presentation-layer protocol) to provide a secure channel over an untrusted network such as the Internet. It was developed by Netscape (SSL 2.0 in 1995, SSL 3.0 in 1996) and was later standardised by the IETF as TLS (Transport Layer Security) — TLS 1.0 (1999), 1.2 (2008), 1.3 (2018). SSL 2.0 and 3.0 are now deprecated and HTTPS uses TLS.

Security services provided
  • Confidentiality — data is encrypted with a negotiated symmetric session key (AES, ChaCha20) so eavesdroppers cannot read it.
  • Integrity — a message authentication code (HMAC/AEAD) detects any modification in transit.
  • Authentication — the server (and optionally the client) proves identity using an X.509 digital certificate signed by a trusted Certificate Authority; the certificate binds the public key to the domain name.
  • Key exchange — asymmetric cryptography (RSA or Diffie-Hellman/ECDHE) safely establishes the shared symmetric key; forward secrecy is obtained with ephemeral DH.
Working (handshake in brief)
  1. ClientHello: the client sends supported TLS version, cipher suites and a random number.
  2. ServerHello + Certificate: the server chooses the cipher suite, sends its certificate and (in older versions) its key-exchange parameters.
  3. Verification: the client validates the certificate chain, dates, and host name against its trust store.
  4. Key exchange: both sides compute the shared pre-master/master secret; the session keys are derived.
  5. Finished: both sides send a Finished message authenticated with the new keys — the secure channel is now open and application data (HTTP, FTP, SMTP...) flows inside it.
  6. Record protocol: during the session, data is fragmented, compressed (optional), authenticated and encrypted; sequence numbers prevent replay.

Where SSL/TLS is used: HTTPS (SSL over HTTP), FTPS, SMTPS, POP3S, IMAPS, LDAP over TLS, VPNs, and any application needing an encrypted socket. Standard ports: HTTPS 443, IMAPS 993, POP3S 995, SMTPS 465/587.

Exam caution: SSL itself is no longer considered secure — always write "SSL/TLS" or "TLS" and mention that modern browsers accept TLS 1.2/1.3 only.
Difference between HTTP and HTTPS
PointHTTPHTTPS
Full formHyperText Transfer ProtocolHyperText Transfer Protocol Secure (HTTP over SSL/TLS)
PortTCP 80 (plain)TCP 443
SecurityNo encryption — data is plain textEncrypted with TLS; confidentiality, integrity, authentication
CertificateNot requiredX.509 digital certificate from a Certificate Authority is required
SpeedSlightly faster (no TLS handshake)Slightly slower on first connection; HTTP/2, HTTP/3 and session resumption largely remove the difference
URL prefixhttp://https:// (padlock icon in the browser)
Data safetyPasswords, card numbers and cookies can be read or modified in transit (MITM attack)Protected against eavesdropping, tampering and server impersonation
SEO / browser behaviourMarked "Not secure" by modern browsers on formsPreferred by search engines; required for geolocation, camera, service workers
Typical usePublic, non-sensitive information pagesLogin, banking, e-commerce, e-mail, APIs, all modern sites

Conclusion: HTTPS = HTTP + TLS. Since almost every site needs authentication and private data, HTTPS is now the default choice; HTTP is retained only for non-sensitive or internal documentation.

Conclusion: HTTP is the simple, stateless, plain-text protocol that transfers Web content on port 80; HTTPS is HTTP protected by SSL/TLS on port 443, adding confidentiality through encryption, integrity through MAC/AEAD and authentication through X.509 certificates. Since browsers mark HTTP pages as “not secure”, require HTTPS for sensitive features and search engines prefer it, HTTPS has become the default for the Web, while HTTP remains only for non-sensitive or internal content.

UNIT 4 — MAIL SERVICES

Long 47
Question

Explain SMTP, DNS, and POP protocol in details.

LongUnit 44.1. Application Layer Services ★
opens in a full-screen window — click the question or press Enter

This answer explains the three protocols of the mail system in detail — SMTP (sending and transferring mail with its command sequence), DNS (the naming service and the MX record lookup that locates the receiver's mail server) and POP3 (downloading mail from the mailbox) — together with the order in which they are used.

Three application-layer protocols work together to deliver and read e-mail: SMTP sends and transfers the message, DNS finds the server that must receive it, and POP3 (or IMAP) lets the receiver download it. Each is explained below in detail.

Definition: SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) is the standard application-layer protocol (RFC 5321) used to send and transfer e-mail messages from a mail client to its mail server and between mail servers. It is a text-based, TCP-based, push protocol; the default port is 25 (port 587 for authenticated submission from clients, 465 for SMTPS).

Working
  1. The client/MUA opens a TCP connection to the mail server on port 25/587.
  2. Both sides greet each other: server sends 220, client sends EHLO (extended SMTP, also negotiates STARTTLS/authentication) or HELO.
  3. The client identifies the sender (MAIL FROM:) and each recipient (RCPT TO:); the server replies 250 for accepted addresses.
  4. The client sends DATA; the server answers 354 and the client sends the header + body, ending with a line containing only a dot (.).
  5. The server replies 250 OK: queued and the client closes the connection with QUIT.
  6. For an external domain, the sender's server looks up the recipient domain's MX record in DNS and repeats the same dialogue with the receiver's server; the message is then stored in the mailbox and later retrieved with POP3 or IMAP.

Features / important points

  • Push (client → server) protocol; not designed for retrieving mail.
  • Reliable, round-robin/queue-based delivery: a copy stays in the queue and retries if the destination server is temporarily unavailable; a bounce message is generated after the retry period expires.
  • Originally 7-bit ASCII only — extended by MIME to carry attachments, non-English text and multiple parts.
  • Extension mechanisms: ESMTP (EHLO), STARTTLS for encryption, AUTH for client login, size extension for large messages.
  • Limitations: no built-in authentication of the sender (spoofing), no encryption by default, no delivery confirmation; hence SPF, DKIM, DMARC and TLS are added. Sending mail directly from a home PC is normally blocked by ISPs (port 25 blocking) — use the ISP/company server on port 587 instead.
Example SMTP session (Telnet to the mail port)
$ telnet mail.example.com 25
220 mail.example.com ESMTP Postfix
EHLO client.example.com
250-mail.example.com
250 OK
MAIL FROM:<[email protected]>
250 2.1.0 Ok
RCPT TO:<[email protected]>
250 2.1.5 Ok
DATA
354 End data with <CR><LF>.<CR><LF>
Subject: Assignment submission

Sir, my assignment is attached.
.
250 2.0.0 Ok: queued as 7F3A21
QUIT
221 2.0.0 Bye

Other useful commands: VRFY (verify a user), RSET (reset the session), NOOP, HELP.

Definition: DNS (Domain Name System) is the distributed, hierarchical naming service of the Internet that translates human-readable domain names into IP addresses (and vice versa). Without DNS users would have to remember numeric IP addresses for every Web site. It is an application-layer service that normally uses UDP port 53 (TCP 53 for large responses and zone transfers).

Hierarchy and components
  • Root servers (13 root server identities, many anycast instances) → TLD servers (.com, .org, .in, .edu) → authoritative name servers of each domain → hosts.
  • DNS resolver (recursive server): the ISP's or company's server that does the work on behalf of the client and caches results.
  • Stub resolver: the small client part in the operating system (configured with the resolver's IP, or 8.8.8.8 / 1.1.1.1).
Main record types
RecordMeaningExample
AMaps a name to an IPv4 addressgtu.ac.in → 14.139.4.10
AAAAMaps a name to an IPv6 addressgtu.ac.in → 2001:db8::1
CNAMEAlias of another namewww → gtu.ac.in
MXMail exchanger — server that accepts mail for the domainmail.gtu.ac.in (priority 10)
NSAuthoritative name server for the zonens1.gtu.ac.in
PTRReverse mapping: IP → name14.139.4.10 → gtu.ac.in
SOAStart of authority: primary server, contact, serial, refresh timers—
TXT / SPF / DKIMText records used for e-mail authentication and verification"v=spf1 include:..."
Resolution types, caching and tools
  • Recursive query: the resolver does all the work and returns the final answer.
  • Iterative query: each server returns a referral to the next server (root → TLD → authoritative) as shown in the figure.
  • Caching: every answer carries a TTL; the resolver and the browser cache it, so repeated lookups are instant and root servers are not overloaded.
  • Tools: nslookup gtu.ac.in, dig gtu.ac.in MX, host gtu.ac.in; the Windows hosts file and ipconfig /displaydns also show cached entries.
  • Zone transfer (AXFR, over TCP 53) replicates the zone between primary and secondary name servers for redundancy.
  • Failures and security: if DNS is down, Web browsing stops even though the network is fine; DNSSEC adds cryptographic signatures, and DNS-over-HTTPS/TLS protects privacy from on-path snooping.

Definition: POP3 (Post Office Protocol version 3, RFC 1939) is the application-layer protocol used by a mail client to download (pull) e-mail messages from the mailbox on the mail server to the local computer. Port 110 (TCP), or 995 for POP3S with TLS.

Working
  1. The client connects to the server on port 110 and authenticates with USER and PASS (or APOP/digest, or TLS).
  2. It asks for the maildrop status (STAT), lists messages (LIST) and retrieves each one (RETR n).
  3. After successful download the client marks or deletes the message (DELE n); QUIT ends the session and the server actually removes the deleted messages.
  4. Typically the messages are then stored on the local disk and read offline; the default behaviour of most clients is store-and-delete.
IMAP (Internet Message Access Protocol)

IMAP4 (RFC 3501) is the modern alternative: port 143 (TCP), or 993 for IMAPS. The mail stays on the server and the client works on it remotely — folders, flags (read/unread/starred), search and synchronisation across phone, tablet and laptop. It supports selective fetching of single parts (e.g. only the text, not a huge attachment) and keeps multiple clients consistent.

POP3 vs IMAP
PointPOP3IMAP
StorageDownloads to the local machine; mail normally removed from serverMail remains on the server
Multi-device usePoor — each device sees only its own copyExcellent — all devices see the same mailboxes
Folder/organisation supportOnly local foldersServer-side folders and flags
Bandwidth on first syncDownloads everythingDownloads headers and only what is opened
Offline readingNatural (mail is local)Supported with client caching
Server storage needLowHigh (but usually free or cheap)
Ports110 / 995 (POP3S)143 / 993 (IMAPS)
Suitable forSingle-device use, low-speed links, archivingSmartphones + laptop + Web mail working together
Sequence of the three protocols in one mail transfer
  1. The sender presses Send; the MUA hands the message to the sender's MTA over SMTP (port 587 with authentication).
  2. The sender's MTA extracts the domain of the recipient and asks DNS for the MX record (port 53), obtaining the IP address of the receiving mail server.
  3. The two MTAs exchange the message over SMTP (EHLO → MAIL FROM → RCPT TO → DATA → 250 queued); the message is stored in the recipient's mailbox.
  4. The recipient's MUA connects to the mail server and retrieves the mail with POP3 (port 110, or 995 with TLS) or with IMAP (143/993).
ProtocolLayerPortDirectionFunction
SMTPApplication25 / 587 / 465PushSend and transfer mail between servers and from clients
DNSApplication53 (UDP/TCP)QueryName → IP resolution, MX/A/PTR records, caching with TTL
POP3Application110 / 995PullDownload mail from the mailbox (store-and-delete)
IMAP (alternative)Application143 / 993Pull/syncRead mail on the server, multi-device synchronisation

Conclusion: SMTP pushes the message, DNS finds the destination server through the MX record, and POP3 pulls the message from the mailbox; together with MIME (for attachments) and TLS (for security) they form the complete e-mail delivery chain. IMAP is the modern alternative to POP3 when the same mailbox must be used from several devices.

Long 49
Question

What is Email? Explain SMTP protocol in detail.

LongUnit 44.1. Application Layer Services ★
opens in a full-screen window — click the question or press Enter

This answer defines e-mail and its components, explains the working of the e-mail system, and then describes SMTP in full detail — its architecture, commands, an example session, features, advantages and limitations.

Definition: Electronic mail (e-mail) is the application-layer service used to compose, send, store, forward and retrieve messages (with optional attachments) between users over a network. It is an asynchronous (store-and-forward) service: the sender and receiver need not be online at the same time.

Components of an e-mail system
  • MUA (Mail User Agent) / e-mail client: the program the user works with — Microsoft Outlook, Mozilla Thunderbird, Apple Mail, Gmail/Outlook Web App. It composes the message, sends it to the mail server and displays the mailbox.
  • MTA (Mail Transfer Agent) / mail server: the server that transfers mail between servers — Sendmail, Postfix, Microsoft Exchange. The sender's MTA pushes the message to the receiver's MTA using SMTP.
  • MDA (Mail Delivery Agent): the program on the receiving server that stores the message in the user's mailbox (Maildir/mbox) and may filter spam.
  • Mailbox and mail store: the storage of the user's messages and folders on the server.
Protocols used in e-mail
ProtocolPortPurpose
SMTP25, 587 (submission), 465 (SMTPS)Push — send/transfer the mail from the client to its server and from server to server.
POP3110, 995 (POP3S)Pull — download mail from the mailbox; normally deletes it from the server (store-and-delete).
IMAP143, 993 (IMAPS)Pull/sync — read mail while it stays on the server; keeps folders and read/unread state in sync across devices.
MIME—Encodes non-ASCII text, attachments and multiple content types inside the SMTP message.
Advantages and disadvantages
  • Advantages: very fast, free or cheap, asynchronous, one message to many recipients (CC/BCC), carries attachments, provides a written record, searchable, accessible from any device, costs nothing extra compared to courier/post for bulk communication.
  • Disadvantages: spam (junk mail), phishing and malware in attachments, no guarantee that the receiver reads it, less personal/friendly than conversation, information overload, reliance on network and server availability, and privacy/monitoring concerns at workplaces.
Working of e-mail — step by step
  1. Composing (MUA): the sender writes the message in the mail client and describes the recipient(s) in the To/Cc/Bcc fields. MIME adds the content type and encodes attachments.
  2. Submission to the sender's server: the MUA sends the message to its own MTA using SMTP (submission port 587 with authentication). A local queue keeps a copy for retry.
  3. DNS lookup: the sender's MTA extracts the domain from the recipient's address and queries DNS for the domain's MX record (Mail eXchanger) to learn which server accepts mail for that domain.
  4. Transfer between servers (SMTP): the sender's MTA opens a TCP connection to the receiver's MTA and delivers the message with the sequence EHLO → MAIL FROM → RCPT TO → DATA → QUIT. If the server is down, the message stays in the queue and the retry is repeated (Hence e-mail is called a store-and-forward service).
  5. Delivery to the mailbox (MDA): the receiver's MTA passes the message to the MDA, which stores it in the recipient's mailbox and may apply spam/virus filters.
  6. Retrieval (POP3/IMAP): the recipient's MUA connects to the mail server and pulls the messages — POP3 usually downloads and deletes them, IMAP keeps them on the server and synchronises folders.
Services provided by an e-mail system
  • Composition, editing and attachment of documents (MIME).
  • Delivery to one or many receivers — To, Cc, Bcc; mailing lists and distribution groups.
  • Storage in folders, searching, flagging, threading of conversations.
  • Reply, reply-all, forward, automatic replies (vacation), read receipts.
  • Address book/contact management, group scheduling and calendars.
  • Security services: spam filtering, virus scanning, DKIM/DMARC authentication, encrypted transport (SMTPS/TLS, POP3S, IMAPS), digital signatures (S/MIME, PGP).
  • Reliable queuing and retry, error/informal messages from the mail server.

Definition: SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) is the standard application-layer protocol (RFC 5321) used to send and transfer e-mail messages from a mail client to its mail server and between mail servers. It is a text-based, TCP-based, push protocol; the default port is 25 (port 587 for authenticated submission from clients, 465 for SMTPS).

Working
  1. The client/MUA opens a TCP connection to the mail server on port 25/587.
  2. Both sides greet each other: server sends 220, client sends EHLO (extended SMTP, also negotiates STARTTLS/authentication) or HELO.
  3. The client identifies the sender (MAIL FROM:) and each recipient (RCPT TO:); the server replies 250 for accepted addresses.
  4. The client sends DATA; the server answers 354 and the client sends the header + body, ending with a line containing only a dot (.).
  5. The server replies 250 OK: queued and the client closes the connection with QUIT.
  6. For an external domain, the sender's server looks up the recipient domain's MX record in DNS and repeats the same dialogue with the receiver's server; the message is then stored in the mailbox and later retrieved with POP3 or IMAP.

Features / important points

  • Push (client → server) protocol; not designed for retrieving mail.
  • Reliable, round-robin/queue-based delivery: a copy stays in the queue and retries if the destination server is temporarily unavailable; a bounce message is generated after the retry period expires.
  • Originally 7-bit ASCII only — extended by MIME to carry attachments, non-English text and multiple parts.
  • Extension mechanisms: ESMTP (EHLO), STARTTLS for encryption, AUTH for client login, size extension for large messages.
  • Limitations: no built-in authentication of the sender (spoofing), no encryption by default, no delivery confirmation; hence SPF, DKIM, DMARC and TLS are added. Sending mail directly from a home PC is normally blocked by ISPs (port 25 blocking) — use the ISP/company server on port 587 instead.
Example SMTP session (Telnet to the mail port)
$ telnet mail.example.com 25
220 mail.example.com ESMTP Postfix
EHLO client.example.com
250-mail.example.com
250 OK
MAIL FROM:<[email protected]>
250 2.1.0 Ok
RCPT TO:<[email protected]>
250 2.1.5 Ok
DATA
354 End data with <CR><LF>.<CR><LF>
Subject: Assignment submission

Sir, my assignment is attached.
.
250 2.0.0 Ok: queued as 7F3A21
QUIT
221 2.0.0 Bye

Other useful commands: VRFY (verify a user), RSET (reset the session), NOOP, HELP.

Conclusion: e-mail is a store-and-forward application service built from MUAs, MTAs, MDAs and mailboxes; SMTP (port 25/587) is the protocol that pushes the message from the sender towards the receiver's server in a simple text dialogue, and POP3/IMAP later deliver it to the recipient. Because SMTP itself is an unauthenticated, plain-text protocol, SPF, DKIM, DMARC and STARTTLS are used in practice to prevent spoofing and to protect the message in transit.

Long 53
Question

Explain E-mail message Components.

LongUnit 44.1. Application Layer Services
opens in a full-screen window — click the question or press Enter

This answer explains the components of an e-mail message in detail — the header fields (From, To, Cc, Bcc, Subject, Date, Message-ID, Reply-To, Received and the MIME fields), the body (text, HTML and attachments encoded in Base64) and the difference between the envelope and the header.

An e-mail message has two main parts: the header (control information) and the body (actual message content), separated by a blank line.

1. Header fields
FieldMeaningExample
FromE-mail address of the senderFrom: [email protected]
ToPrimary recipient address(es) — visible to all receiversTo: [email protected]
Cc (Carbon copy)Additional recipients; all recipients can see this listCc: [email protected]
Bcc (Blind carbon copy)Hidden recipients; their addresses are not shown to othersBcc: [email protected]
SubjectShort description of the message contentSubject: NT-503 question bank
DateDate and time the message was composedDate: Thu, 2 Oct 2026 10:15:00 +0530
Message-IDUnique identifier of this message, added by the first mail server<[email protected]>
Reply-ToAddress to which replies should be sent, if different from FromReply-To: [email protected]
ReceivedTrace of every server that handled the message (added by each MTA)Received: from ...
MIME-Version, Content-Type, Content-Transfer-EncodingTell the client the message format and how the body/attachment is encodedContent-Type: text/html; charset=UTF-8
In-Reply-To / ReferencesMessage-ID of the message being answered (used for threading)In-Reply-To: <[email protected]>
2. Body
  • The actual content — plain text (ASCII), HTML (formatted with fonts, colours, tables, links) or both (multipart/alternative; the client chooses the best it can display).
  • Attachments are separate MIME parts (Content-Disposition: attachment) encoded in Base64 so binary files (PDF, DOCX, JPG, ZIP) can travel through a text-only mail system.
  • A signature block at the end (name, designation, contact details) is a convention, not a protocol field.
Envelope vs header

The envelope is the information used by SMTP servers to deliver the message (MAIL FROM: and RCPT TO:) and is not visible to the user; the header is the user-visible information stored inside the message. A message can be addressed to someone in RCPT TO even when the Bcc header is empty — this is why Bcc works.

Example of a complete message
From: [email protected]
To: [email protected]
Cc: [email protected]
Bcc: [email protected]
Subject: Submission of Network Technology assignment
Date: Thu, 02 Oct 2026 10:15:00 +0530
Message-ID: <[email protected]>
MIME-Version: 1.0
Content-Type: multipart/mixed; boundary="==BOUNDARY=="

--==BOUNDARY==
Content-Type: text/plain; charset="UTF-8"

Sir, please find my assignment attached.
--==BOUNDARY==
Content-Type: application/pdf; name="nt503.pdf"
Content-Transfer-Encoding: base64

JVBERi0xLjQKJcOkw7zDtsO...   (Base64 data)
--==BOUNDARY==--

Conclusion: an e-mail message is a header plus a body separated by a blank line: the header carries the addressing and trace information (From, To, Cc, Bcc, Subject, Date, Message-ID, MIME fields), and the body carries the text/HTML content and the Base64-encoded attachments defined by MIME. The envelope (MAIL FROM / RCPT TO) is what SMTP uses for delivery and is hidden from the user — which is exactly why Bcc recipients can receive a copy without appearing in the header.

Long 54
Question

Define URL. Give examples of it. Explain types of URL.

LongUnit 44.1.3. URL and URL Types ★★
opens in a full-screen window — click the question or press Enter

This answer defines the URL, shows its full syntax and components with examples, and explains the types of URL — absolute, relative, root-relative, static, dynamic, canonical and protocol-specific — with the difference between URL, URI and URN.

Definition: A URL (Uniform Resource Locator) is the complete address that identifies the location of a resource (Web page, image, file, video, API) on the Internet and the protocol used to access it. It is a type of URI (Uniform Resource Identifier): a URI identifies a resource, a URL tells where to find it, and a URN (Uniform Resource Name) names a resource permanently without giving its location.

General syntax

scheme://host:port/path/filename?query#fragment

ComponentMeaningExample
Scheme (protocol)How to access the resourcehttp, https, ftp, file, mailto
Authority / hostDomain name or IP of the server (optionally user:password@ before it)www.example.com
PortServer port; default is hidden (80 for HTTP, 443 for HTTPS):8080
PathDirectory/folder structure of the resource on the server/courses/net503/
File nameThe particular resourceindex.html
Query stringData sent to the server/program, starts with "?"; pairs joined by "&"?unit=1&topic=osi
Fragment (anchor)Point inside the document, starts with "#"#layers
Examples
  • https://www.gtu.ac.in/index.html — the GTU home page over secure HTTP.
  • ftp://ftp.gnu.org/gnu/bash/ — directory of files on an FTP server.
  • mailto:[email protected] — starts a new mail message.
  • https://www.google.com/search?q=osi+model — a search query passed to a Web application.
Types of URL
  1. Absolute URL — contains the full scheme and host; works from anywhere: https://www.example.com/images/logo.png.
  2. Relative URL — contains only the path; resolved against the current page: /images/logo.png, ../notes/ch1.pdf, contact.html.
  3. Root-relative URL — begins with "/", resolved from the site root: /courses/index.html.
  4. Static URL — points to a fixed file that exists on the server (/about.html); Dynamic URL — contains parameters and generates the page from a database (/product.php?id=1024).
  5. Canonical URL — the single preferred address for a page when several URLs show the same content (chosen to avoid duplicate-content problems).
  6. Protocol-specific URLs — http://, https://, ftp://, file:/// for a local file, mailto:, tel:.

Conclusion: a URL is the complete, standardised address of a resource on the Internet — scheme, host, port, path, query and fragment — and it is the mechanism by which browsers, search engines, e-mail clients and applications locate Web pages, files and services. Its types (absolute/relative, static/dynamic, canonical) are used in Web development and SEO, and the URL is one kind of URI, the other being the URN.

It is a type of URI (Uniform Resource Identifier): a URI identifies a resource, a URL tells where to find it, and a URN (Uniform Resource Name) names a resource permanently without giving its location.

General syntax

scheme://host:port/path/filename?query#fragment

ComponentMeaningExample
Scheme (protocol)How to access the resourcehttp, https, ftp, file, mailto
Authority / hostDomain name or IP of the server (optionally user:password@ before it)www.example.com
PortServer port; default is hidden (80 for HTTP, 443 for HTTPS):8080
PathDirectory/folder structure of the resource on the server/courses/net503/
File nameThe particular resourceindex.html
Query stringData sent to the server/program, starts with "?"; pairs joined by "&"?unit=1&topic=osi
Fragment (anchor)Point inside the document, starts with "#"#layers
Examples
  • https://www.gtu.ac.in/index.html — the GTU home page over secure HTTP.
  • ftp://ftp.gnu.org/gnu/bash/ — directory of files on an FTP server.
  • mailto:[email protected] — starts a new mail message.
  • https://www.google.com/search?q=osi+model — a search query passed to a Web application.
Types of URL
  1. Absolute URL — contains the full scheme and host; works from anywhere: https://www.example.com/images/logo.png.
  2. Relative URL — contains only the path; resolved against the current page: /images/logo.png, ../notes/ch1.pdf, contact.html.
  3. Root-relative URL — begins with "/", resolved from the site root: /courses/index.html.
  4. Static URL — points to a fixed file that exists on the server (/about.html); Dynamic URL — contains parameters and generates the page from a database (/product.php?id=1024).
  5. Canonical URL — the single preferred address for a page when several URLs show the same content (chosen to avoid duplicate-content problems).
  6. Protocol-specific URLs — http://, https://, ftp://, file:/// for a local file, mailto:, tel:.

Conclusion: a URL consists of a scheme (http, https, ftp), the host (domain or IP), an optional port, a path, a query string and a fragment; URLs may be absolute or relative, static or dynamic, and canonical for a preferred page address. They are the glue of the World Wide Web — every link, bookmark, search result and API call is a URL.

Question

Write a Case Study of Steps and protocols involved in accessing URL.

LongUnit 44.1.3. URL and URL Types

This case study follows a user who types https://www.example.com/courses/index.html and describes every step and protocol involved — URL parsing, cache lookup, DNS resolution, ARP, the TCP three-way handshake, the TLS handshake, the HTTP request and response, rendering of sub-resources and connection persistence.

Definition: A URL (Uniform Resource Locator) is the complete address that identifies the location of a resource (Web page, image, file, video, API) on the Internet and the protocol used to access it. It is a type of URI (Uniform Resource Identifier): a URI identifies a resource, a URL tells where to find it, and a URN (Uniform Resource Name) names a resource permanently without giving its location.

General syntax

scheme://host:port/path/filename?query#fragment

ComponentMeaningExample
Scheme (protocol)How to access the resourcehttp, https, ftp, file, mailto
Authority / hostDomain name or IP of the server (optionally user:password@ before it)www.example.com
PortServer port; default is hidden (80 for HTTP, 443 for HTTPS):8080
PathDirectory/folder structure of the resource on the server/courses/net503/
File nameThe particular resourceindex.html
Query stringData sent to the server/program, starts with "?"; pairs joined by "&"?unit=1&topic=osi
Fragment (anchor)Point inside the document, starts with "#"#layers
Examples
  • https://www.gtu.ac.in/index.html — the GTU home page over secure HTTP.
  • ftp://ftp.gnu.org/gnu/bash/ — directory of files on an FTP server.
  • mailto:[email protected] — starts a new mail message.
  • https://www.google.com/search?q=osi+model — a search query passed to a Web application.
Types of URL
  1. Absolute URL — contains the full scheme and host; works from anywhere: https://www.example.com/images/logo.png.
  2. Relative URL — contains only the path; resolved against the current page: /images/logo.png, ../notes/ch1.pdf, contact.html.
  3. Root-relative URL — begins with "/", resolved from the site root: /courses/index.html.
  4. Static URL — points to a fixed file that exists on the server (/about.html); Dynamic URL — contains parameters and generates the page from a database (/product.php?id=1024).
  5. Canonical URL — the single preferred address for a page when several URLs show the same content (chosen to avoid duplicate-content problems).
  6. Protocol-specific URLs — http://, https://, ftp://, file:/// for a local file, mailto:, tel:.
Case study: steps and protocols involved in accessing a URL

Suppose a user types https://www.example.com/courses/index.html in a browser. The following steps take place (each with its protocol):

  1. URL parsing (HTTP/HTTPS): the browser splits the URL into scheme (https), host (www.example.com), path (/courses/index.html).
  2. Cache check: the browser looks in its own cache and the OS DNS cache for the site and the page. If the page is fresh (Cache-Control/Expires headers), it is displayed without any network request.
  3. DNS resolution (DNS, UDP/TCP 53): the stub resolver asks the configured recursive resolver; the resolver queries the root server, the .com TLD server and the domain's authoritative server, obtains the A record (IP address) and caches it for the TTL period.
  4. Address resolution (ARP): for the gateway on the local LAN the host needs a MAC address; ARP broadcasts "who has 192.168.1.1?" and caches the reply. (IPv6 uses neighbour discovery.)
  5. TCP connection (TCP, port 443): the browser performs the three-way handshake — SYN → SYN+ACK → ACK — with the Web server. TCP provides the reliable byte stream used by HTTP.
  6. TLS handshake (TLS 1.2/1.3): for HTTPS, the server sends its X.509 certificate; the client verifies it against a trusted CA and the host name, both sides agree on cipher suites and derive session keys using ECDHE, and the encrypted tunnel is established. (For plain HTTP this step is skipped and the port is 80.)
  7. HTTP request: the browser sends the request line and headers — GET /courses/index.html HTTP/1.1, Host: www.example.com, User-Agent, Accept, Accept-Encoding, Cookie, Connection: keep-alive.
  8. Server processing: the Web server (Apache/Nginx) or application server locates the file or runs the program, consults the database if needed and builds the response.
  9. HTTP response: HTTP/1.1 200 OK with headers (Content-Type: text/html; charset=UTF-8, Content-Length, Cache-Control, Set-Cookie, ETag) and the HTML body. Error cases: 301/302 redirect (browser re-requests the new URL), 404 Not Found, 500 Server Error.
  10. Rendering and sub-resources: the browser parses the HTML and requests the CSS, JavaScript, images and fonts — with HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 these are multiplexed over one connection, and some may come from the cache or a CDN.
  11. Persistence: with keep-alive (HTTP/1.1) or multiplexing (HTTP/2, HTTP/3 over QUIC/UDP) the same connection is reused for further requests; cookies and session IDs keep the user logged in although HTTP itself is stateless.
Protocols involved at a glance: DNS (name → IP), ARP (IP → MAC), TCP (reliable transport, handshake), TLS (encryption and authentication), HTTP/HTTPS (the request and the response), plus DHCP earlier when the host obtained its own IP address.

Conclusion: a single click on a URL hides a chain of protocols — DNS gives the IP address, ARP gives the MAC address, TCP provides the reliable connection, TLS secures it, and HTTP carries the request and the response, after which the browser renders the page. Understanding this sequence explains where problems occur (a wrong DNS entry, a blocked port, an expired certificate, a 404 page) and is one of the most frequently examined topics of this unit.

Long 58
Question

What is search Engine? Explain the process of locating website.

LongUnit 44.3. Case Study of Locating Website / Search Engine ★★★
opens in a full-screen window — click the question or press Enter

This answer defines the search engine, describes its components (crawler, indexer, query processor, ranking algorithm, user interface), explains how a search engine works, and then follows the complete process of locating a website — from the query to the rendered page.

Definition: A search engine is a Web-based software system that helps users find information on the World Wide Web. The user types keywords or a question (a query); the search engine matches the query against its own pre-built index of Web pages and returns a ranked list of results with the page title, URL and a short snippet. Popular examples: Google, Bing, Yahoo, DuckDuckGo, Baidu, Yandex.

Components of a search engine
ComponentFunction
Crawler / spider / robot (e.g. Googlebot)Automatically visits pages starting from seed URLs and sitemaps, follows the links found on each page and brings back the page content; respects robots.txt.
Indexer / indexer-databaseParses the fetched pages, removes formatting, extracts words, links, images and metadata, and stores them in an inverted index (word → list of documents).
Query processor / search algorithmParses the user's query, expands synonyms, finds matching documents in the index and ranks them.
Ranking algorithmOrders results by relevance: keyword match and location, page authority (PageRank-style link analysis), freshness, HTTPS, mobile-friendliness, page speed, user engagement.
User interfaceThe search box and the results page, plus filters (images, videos, news, maps, time range) and ads.
Process of locating a website with a search engine (step by step)
  1. User enters a query in the search box, e.g. "GTU network technology syllabus".
  2. Query processing: the engine tokenises the words, corrects spelling, removes stop words, expands synonyms and may use the user's location/language.
  3. Index lookup: the inverted index is searched for the query terms; the engine gets the list of candidate documents containing them (this is why the reply is almost instant — the Web is not searched live).
  4. Ranking: candidates are scored with hundreds of signals — term frequency and position, anchor text, number and quality of inbound links, page freshness, site trust, HTTPS, load speed, and personalisation.
  5. Result page (SERP): the ranked list is formatted with title, URL, snippet and rich results (images, reviews, maps, "People also ask"); the best answer may appear in a featured snippet or knowledge panel.
  6. User clicks a result → the browser accesses that URL: DNS resolution → TCP connection → TLS (if https) → HTTP GET → the Web server returns the page → the browser renders it. This is the same URL-access case study described in the previous section.
  7. Feedback: the engine records the click (CTR), dwell time and pogo-sticking, and later uses fresh crawls of the site to update the index — this is the basis of SEO (Search Engine Optimisation).
Search operators, advantages and limitations
  • Handy operators: "exact phrase", site:gtu.ac.in, filetype:pdf, intitle:topology, -unwanted, OR.
  • Advantages: finds relevant pages among billions, instant results, free, works in every language, adds maps, images, news, videos, shopping, and can answer direct questions.
  • Limitations: results depend on the algorithm and can be manipulated by SEO spam; not all pages are indexed (deep Web, login-protected pages); privacy issues (queries are logged/profiled); ads compete with the real results; a crawler may show outdated content; SEO-friendly wording is needed for a site to be found.
  • How to get a website listed: publish it on a public server with a domain name, allow crawlers in robots.txt, submit the sitemap/URL to the search engine, link it from other sites, and keep the content unique and well-structured (titles, headings, meta description, HTTPS).

Conclusion: a search engine works in four stages — crawling the Web, building an inverted index, matching and ranking the user's query, and presenting the result page — after which locating the website is the URL-access process (DNS → TCP → TLS → HTTP → rendering). Search engines have made the Web usable at its present scale, although their ranking algorithms, advertisements and privacy implications must be understood critically.
